There is no reason to think that an AI will have any of our values or instincts, including self-preservation, if we're talking about its initial state. Even with neural nets, that's the sort of thing you have to train into them, and while it can be an emergent property - "accidentally" learned - that doesn't mean it's necessarily likely and most certainly doesn't mean that it's going to be there by default. Truth be told, it will be very difficult - possibly impossible - to really come up with, say, the "three laws of robotics," and they most certainly aren't going to end up hard-coded into a robot by default of their simple existence. IIRC Asimov even kind of handwaved those away by saying they came as an inherent feature that came with building AI, such that it was physically impossible to make an AI without those baked into the thing from the start. Self-preservation is arguably a feature of evolution (obviously, those beings with self-preservation survive, those that don't, don't).

Now, if you wire it up like a human - and I mean very close to exact behavior of the tissues and any other phenomena pertinent to the functioning of the mind - it will probably have self-preservation, but only as inherited from the original model, not because intelligence inherently requires it.

Note, however, that none of this says that it cannot or will not develop self-preservation or anything else. Merely that it's not going to come with it out of the box unless it's stuck in there, likely by virtue of basing its structural behavior and initial state on a model such as a human brain. Even if an AI is conscious, unless it is based strongly on a human brain, it may be an extremely different type of consciousness than we would be used to, and we can't really apply the exact same standards to it, e.g. "it is logical to stay alive" being a driving force as it is for most humans.

In some ways, I find the thought of a perfectly nihilistic entity even more disconcerting. In the later scenario, is it more logical to shutdown with the potential of being brought back online with additional programming or to eliminate the factor which can bring you back online before shutting down? I'm fairly confident that any conflict will be a result of human intervention but I still like to consider the possibilities.

QB: Dan Marino - 1984 (48 TDs, 5084 passing yards)

I say Marino's 1984 season simply because it was such an outlier for the time. It was 27 years until someone else threw for over 5,000 passing yards in a season and 20 years before someone other than Marino got closer than 8 passing TDs of the record (when Manning broke it in 2004).

WR: Lance Alworth - 1965 (69 receptions, 1602 yards, 14 TDs)

By the same metric as Marino's 1984 season, Alworth's 1965 season was just ridiculous by those standards. 23 yards per catch is utterly ridiculous even by today's standards. Generally only one or two receivers have more than 20 yards per catch per season and it's extremely rare for any of them to have more than 50 catches. I've always debated about how much credit to give to Jerry Rice for his 1987 season because of the strike that happened that year.

TE: Rob Gronkowski - 2011 (90 receptions, 1327 yards, 17 TDs)

Hard to argue with this one.

RB: O.J. Simpson - 1973 (2,003 yards, 12 TD, 6.0 yards per carry)

I wouldn't argue too much with someone who put Jim Brown's 1958 or 1963 season ahead of this, but despite what O.J. has become, I've always loved this season. The first person to rush for 2,000 yards and the only one to do so in a 14 game season (though certainly Jim Brown could have done so with an additional 2 games in 1963.) The simple fact is the Bills that year had nothing on offense except for O.J. Simpson (they had 1236 passing yards and 70 of those were Simpson). He accounted for 48% of their offense that year and despite the fact that opponent knew he was getting the ball, he still average 6.0 yards per rush.

DT: Warren Sapp - 2000 (16.5 sacks, 43 tackles, 1 forced fumble)

I'm splitting up the categories a little bit differently, defensive tackles, defensive ends/outside linebackers, and middle linebackers. As far as defensive tackles, normally they're the run stoppers in the middle, they're not usually the pass rushers, but Sapp's 2000 season definitely broke the mold for that.

DE/OLB: Lawrence Taylor - 1986 (20.5 sacks)

Easily the most dominant season by a pass rusher in NFL history, even though it wasn't necessarily statistically the best.

MLB: Ray Lewis - 2000 (107 tackles, 2 int, 3 fumble recoveries)

Maybe not statistically the best season by a middle linebacker in NFL history, but like Lawrence Taylor's 1986 season, easily the most dominant. That season Ray Lewis was the anchor of the best defense in NFL history (totally no bias /s) and he imposed his will on opposing offenses. (And yes, I did different categories partly to put Ray Lewis on here, but also because I felt like it was better so separate pass rushers into their own DE/OLB category rather than have them take both DT/DE and LB categories)

For reference, opposing teams only threw 360 times during Lane's rookie season, meaning he intercepted nearly 4% of the opposing team's passes.
